en: Taal Volcano produces violent explosions when rising hot magma directly contacts the cool water of its main crater lake.
The Habagat monsoon drops heavy rain because moist winds from the West Philippine Sea release water when hitting mountains.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River formed over millions of years as slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved the underground limestone bedrock.
The step-like structure of the Banaue Rice Terraces prevents soil erosion by slowing down rainwater runoff flowing down the mountains.
Geothermal power plants in Tiwi generate electricity by using naturally heated underground steam from volcanoes to spin large turbines.
The Chocolate Hills in Bohol turn brown during the dry season because the lack of rainfall causes the covering grass to dry out.
Typhoons gain immense strength over the Pacific Ocean because warm seawater evaporates rapidly, transferring heat energy into the storm system.
The Tubbataha Reefs continuously grow because tiny coral polyps extract dissolved calcium carbonate from the clear seawater to build hard skeletons.
Taal Lake exists today because a massive ancient volcanic eruption collapsed the summit, creating a large caldera that later filled with rainwater.
The Mount Makiling forest watershed supplies clean water to nearby provinces because tree roots absorb rain and slowly filter it into springs.
The Cagayan River delta expands into the sea because the slow-moving water deposits carried soil and sediment at its mouth.
The San Bernardino Strait experiences very strong ocean currents because the massive volume of water is forced through a narrow gap between islands.
